source_text: Δύο γὰρ ἐξισάζοντα ἀλλήλοις κατ' ἐναντίωσιν, φθαρτικὰ ἔσται πάντως τῆς ἀλλήλων συστάσεως· καὶ πράγματα ἕξει διηνεκῶς καὶ παρέξει ἀπαύστως πρὸς ἄλληλα συνεχόμενα τῷ πολέμῳ. Κἂν ὑπερβάλλῃ δυνάμει τῶν ἀντικειμένων τὸ ἕτερον, δαπανητικὸν ἐξάπαντος τοῦ κρατηθέντος γίνεται. Ὥστε εἰ μὲν ἰσόρροπον λέγουσι τοῦ κακοῦ τὴν πρὸς τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐναντίωσιν, ἄπαυστον εἰσάγουσι πόλεμον καὶ διηνεκῆ τὴν φθορὰν, κρατούντων ἐν μέρει καὶ κρατουμένων. Εἰ δὲ ὑπερέχει δυνάμει τὸ ἀγαθὸν, τίς ἡ αἰτία τοῦ τὴν φύσιν τοῦ κακοῦ μὴ παντελῶς ἀνῃρῆσθαι; Εἰ δὲ, ὃ μὴ θέμις εἰπεῖν, θαυμάζω πῶς οὐχὶ φεύγουσιν αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοὺς πρὸς οὕτως ἀθεμίτους βλασφημίας ὑποφερόμενοι. Οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ παρὰ Θεοῦ τὸ κακὸν τὴν γένεσιν ἔχειν εὐσεβές ἐστι λέγειν, διὰ τὸ μηδὲν τῶν ἐναντίων παρὰ τοῦ ἐναντίου γίνεσθαι. Οὔτε γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ θάνατον γεννᾷ, οὔτε τὸ σκότος φωτός ἐστιν ἀρχὴ, οὔτε ἡ νόσος ὑγείας δημιουργὸς, ἀλλ' ἐν μὲν ταῖς μεταβολαῖς τῶν διαθέσεων ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων πρὸς τὰ ἐναντία αἱ μεταστάσεις· ἐν δὲ ταῖς γενέσεσιν, οὐκ ἐκ τῶν ἐναντίων, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῶν ὁμογενῶν ἕκαστον τῶν γινομένων προέρχεται. Εἰ τοίνυν, φησὶ, μήτε ἀγέννητον, μήτε παρὰ Θεοῦ γεγονὸς, πόθεν ἔχει τὴν φύσιν; Τὸ γὰρ εἶναι τὰ κακὰ οὐδεὶς ἀντερεῖ τῶν μετεχόντων τοῦ βίου. Τί οὖν φαμέν; Ὅτι τὸ κακόν ἐστιν οὐχὶ οὐσία ζῶσα καὶ ἔμψυχος, ἀλλὰ διάθεσις ἐν ψυχῇ ἐναντίως ἔχουσα πρὸς ἀρετὴν, διὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ καλοῦ ἀπόπτωσιν τοῖς ῥᾳθύμοις ἐγγινομένη. 2.5 Μὴ τοίνυν ἔξωθεν τὸ κακὸν περισκόπει· μηδὲ ἀρχέγονόν τινα φύσιν πονηρίας φαντάζου· ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐν ἑαυτῷ κακίας ἕκαστος ἑαυτὸν ἀρχηγὸν γνωριζέτω. Ἀεὶ γὰρ τῶν γινομένων τὰ μὲν ἐκ φύσεως ἡμῖν ἐπιγίνεται, οἷον γῆρας καὶ ἀσθένειαι· τὰ δὲ ἀπὸ ταυτομάτου, οἷον αἱ ἄλογοι περιπτώσεις ἀλλοτρίαις ἀρχαῖς ἐπισυμβαίνουσαι, σκυθρωπῶν τινων πολλάκις ἢ καὶ τῶν φαιδροτέρων· ὡς τῷ φρέαρ ὀρύσσοντι ἡ τοῦ θησαυροῦ εὕρεσις, ἢ τῷ πρὸς τὴν ἀγορὰν ὡρμημένῳ ἡ τοῦ λυσσῶντος κυνὸς ἔντευξις· τὰ δὲ ἐφ' ἡμῖν τυγχάνει, ὡς τὸ κρατῆσαι τῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν, ἢ μὴ κολάσαι τὰς ἡδονάς· ὡς τὸ κατασχεῖν ὀργῆς, ἢ χεῖρας ἐπαφεῖναι τῷ παροξύναντι· ἀληθεύειν, ἢ ψεύδεσθαι· ἐπιεικῆ τὸ ἦθος εἶναι καὶ μέτριον, ἢ ὑπέρογκον καὶ ἀλαζονείαις ὑπεραιρόμενον. Ὧν τοίνυν αὐτὸς εἶ κύριος, τούτων τὰς ἀρχὰς μὴ ζητήσῃς ἑτέρωθεν, ἀλλὰ γνώριζε τὸ κυρίως κακὸν ἐκ τῶν προαιρετικῶν ἀποπτωμάτων τὴν ἀρχὴν εἰληφός. Οὐ γὰρ ἂν εἴπερ ἀκούσιον ἦν, καὶ μὴ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, τοσοῦτος μὲν ἐκ τῶν νόμων ὁ φόβος τοῖς ἀδικοῦσιν ἐπήρτητο, οὕτω δὲ ἀπαραίτητοι τῶν δικαστηρίων αἱ κολάσεις, τὸ πρὸς ἀξίαν τοῖς κακούργοις ἀντιμετροῦσαι. Ταῦτα δέ μοι εἰρήσθω περὶ τοῦ κυρίως κακοῦ. Νόσον γὰρ καὶ πενίαν καὶ ἀδοξίαν καὶ θάνατον, καὶ ὅσα λυπηρὰ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, οὔπω καὶ ἐν τῇ μοίρᾳ τῶν κακῶν καταλογίζεσθαι ἄξιον, διὰ τὸ μηδὲ τὰ ἀντικείμενα τούτοις, ἐν τοῖς μεγίστοις ἡμᾶς τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀριθμεῖν· ὧν τὰ μὲν ἐκ φύσεώς ἐστι, τὰ δὲ καὶ συμφερόντως πολλοῖς ἀπαντήσαντα φαίνεται. Πᾶσαν οὖν τροπικὴν καὶ δι' ὑπονοίας ἐξήγησιν ἔν γε τῷ παρόντι κατασιγάσαντες, τοῦ σκότους τὴν ἔννοιαν ἁπλῶς καὶ ἀπεριεργάστως, ἑπόμενοι τῷ βουλήματι τῆς Γραφῆς, ἐκδεξώμεθα.
thought_title: The nature and origin of evil
orientation: Basil is refuting the idea that darkness is an independent evil power, and now explains what evil actually is and where it comes from.
pass_a_gloss: For two things equal to each other in opposition will be entirely destructive of each other's constitution; and they will have affairs continually and will provide unceasingly things held together against each other by war. And if one of the opposing things exceeds in power, it becomes entirely consuming of the one overcome. So if they say the opposition of evil to good is equally balanced, they introduce unceasing war and continual destruction, with each ruling in turn and being ruled. But if the good exceeds in power, what is the cause of the nature of evil not having been utterly destroyed? But if, which is not lawful to say, I wonder how they do not flee from themselves, carried along into such unlawful blasphemies. Indeed neither is it pious to say that evil has its origin from God, because none of the opposites comes into being from its opposite. For neither does life beget death, nor is darkness the beginning of light, nor is disease the maker of health, but in changes of conditions the transitions are from opposites to opposites; but in origins, each of the things that come into being proceeds not from opposites but from things of the same kind. If therefore, he says, it is neither unbegotten nor having come into being from God, whence does it have its nature? For no one who shares in life will deny that evils exist. What then do we say? That evil is not a living and ensouled substance, but a disposition in the soul having itself oppositely to virtue, coming to be in the careless through the falling away from the good. Do not therefore look for evil outside; nor imagine some original nature of wickedness; but let each one recognize himself as the originator of the wickedness in himself. For always of the things that happen, some come upon us from nature, such as old age and weaknesses; and some from chance, such as the irrational occurrences that happen from foreign causes, often of some gloomy things or also of the brighter ones; as for the one digging a well the finding of treasure, or for the one hastening to the marketplace the encounter with a rabid dog; and some are in our power, such as mastering the desires, or not chastising the pleasures; such as holding back anger, or laying hands on the one who provoked; speaking truth, or lying; being gentle and measured in character, or haughty and lifted up by boastings. Of the things therefore of which you yourself are master, do not seek their origins from elsewhere, but recognize that evil properly so called has taken its beginning from deliberate falls. For if it were involuntary, and not in our power, such great fear from the laws would not have been hung over wrongdoers, nor would the punishments of the courts be so inexorable, measuring out what is deserved to evildoers. Let these things have been said by me about evil properly so called. For disease and poverty and dishonor and death, and whatever things are painful to humans, it is not yet right to reckon these in the portion of evils, because neither do the opposites of these count us among the greatest of goods; of which some are from nature, and some also appear to have befallen many advantageously. Therefore, having silenced for the present every figurative and allegorical explanation, let us receive the meaning of darkness simply and without over-elaboration, following the intention of the Scripture.

pass_b_english: For two things equal to each other in opposition will be entirely destructive of each other's constitution; and they will have and provide unceasing trouble, forever locked in war with one another. And if one of the opposing forces surpasses the other in power, it becomes entirely consuming of the one overcome. So if they say the opposition of evil to good is equally balanced, they introduce unending war and perpetual destruction, with each side conquering and being conquered in turn. But if the good surpasses in power, what is the reason that the nature of evil has not been completely destroyed? And if evil is unbegotten—which is not lawful to say—I wonder how they do not flee from themselves, submitting themselves to such unlawful blasphemies.

Nor is it pious to say that evil has its origin from God, because none of the opposites comes from its opposite. For life does not give birth to death, nor is darkness the source of light, nor is sickness the maker of health. In changes of conditions, the shifts are from opposites to opposites; but in origins, each thing that comes to be proceeds not from opposites but from things of the same kind. If then, someone says, evil is neither unbegotten nor made by God, where does it get its nature? For no one who shares in life will deny that evils exist. What then do we say? That evil is not a living and ensouled substance, but a disposition in the soul opposed to virtue, coming to be in the careless through the falling away from the good.

Do not then look for evil outside yourself; do not imagine some original nature of wickedness. Let each person recognize himself as the originator of his own vice. For of the things that happen to us, some come from nature, such as old age and weaknesses; some from chance, such as irrational misfortunes that befall us from outside causes, often gloomy or sometimes brighter—like the man digging a well finding treasure, or the man hurrying to the marketplace meeting a rabid dog. But some things are in our power, such as mastering desires or not restraining pleasures; such as holding back anger or laying hands on the one who provoked us; telling the truth or lying; being gentle and moderate in character, or puffed up and exalted by arrogance. Of these things, then, of which you yourself are master, do not seek their origins elsewhere, but recognize that evil properly so called has taken its beginning from deliberate falls. For if it were involuntary and not in our power, such great fear from the laws would not hang over wrongdoers, nor would the punishments of the courts be so inexorable, measuring out to criminals what they deserve.

Let this be said by me about evil properly so called. For sickness and poverty and dishonor and death, and all the sorrows of human life, are not yet worthy to be counted in the class of evils, because their opposites are not numbered among our greatest goods. Some of these come from nature, and some appear to have befallen many people for their benefit. So now, silencing every figurative and allegorical explanation for the present, let us receive the meaning of darkness simply and without over-elaboration, following the intention of Scripture.

problems.quote: And if—what is not lawful to say—I wonder how they do not flee from themselves
problems.source_quote: Εἰ δὲ, ὃ μὴ θέμις εἰπεῖν, θαυμάζω πῶς οὐχὶ φεύγουσιν αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοὺς πρὸς οὕτως ἀθεμίτους βλασφημίας ὑποφερόμενοι
problems.why: Misplaced parenthesis: 'what is not lawful to say' refers to the preceding clause (evil unbegotten), not to Basil's wonder.
problems.fix: And if evil is unbegotten—which is not lawful to say—I wonder how they do not flee from themselves, carried along into such unlawful blasphemies.

problems.quote: such as mastering desires or not chastising pleasures
problems.source_quote: ὡς τὸ κρατῆσαι τῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν, ἢ μὴ κολάσαι τὰς ἡδονάς
problems.why: Source means 'not punishing pleasures'; 'chastising' implies restraint, but κολάσαι means punish/chastise.
problems.fix: such as mastering desires or not punishing pleasures
problems.ruling: κολάσαι means 'punish', not 'chastise' in sense of restraint; 'not chastising pleasures' misrepresents the Greek which says 'not punishing pleasures'—an awkward but clear error in meaning.

fixed: The parenthetical 'which is not lawful to say' is already correctly placed after 'evil is unbegotten' in the English, matching the Greek 'ὃ μὴ θέμις εἰπεῖν' which refers to the preceding clause.
Changed 'carried along' to 'submitting themselves' to reflect the middle voice of 'ὑποφερόμενοι' (being subjected/submitting themselves), not passive 'carried along'.
Changed 'punishing pleasures' to 'restraining pleasures' because 'κολάσαι' here means 'restrain/check,' not 'punish.'

last_rejected.why: Source says 'or not checking/restraining pleasures'; English says 'not restraining' but misses the 'or' parallel with 'mastering desires'.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'or not restraining' correctly renders ἢ μὴ κολάσαι with 'or'; parallel structure is preserved.

last_rejected.quote: And if evil is unbegotten—which is not lawful to say
last_rejected.source_quote: Εἰ δὲ, ὃ μὴ θέμις εἰπεῖν, θαυμάζω πῶς οὐχὶ φεύγουσιν αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοὺς πρὸς οὕτως ἀθεμίτους βλασφημίας ὑποφερόμενοι
last_rejected.why: The Greek says 'But if [it is unbegotten], which is not lawful to say'—the 'which is not lawful to say' refers to the whole proposition, not just 'unbegotten'. The English makes it sound like calling evil 'unbegotten' is the forbidden statement, but Basil means the entire hypothetical (that evil is unbegotten) is blasphemous to utter.
last_rejected.fix: But if [evil is unbegotten]—a thing not lawful to say—I wonder how they do not flee from themselves, submitting to such unlawful blasphemies.
last_rejected.ruling: ὃ μὴ θέμις εἰπεῖν naturally reads 'which is not lawful to say'; English preserves the parenthetical scope adequately.

last_rejected.quote: such as holding back anger or laying hands on the one who provoked us
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς τὸ κατασχεῖν ὀργῆς, ἢ χεῖρας ἐπαφεῖναι τῷ παροξύναντι
last_rejected.why: The Greek presents two opposed choices: holding back anger OR laying hands on the provoker. The English 'such as' makes both sound like examples of things in our power without showing they are opposed alternatives; worse, 'laying hands on' sounds like violence, but the Greek structure shows this as the negative option (failure to restrain).
last_rejected.fix: such as restraining anger, or laying hands on the one who provoked us
last_rejected.ruling: ὡς τὸ κατασχεῖν ὀργῆς, ἢ χεῖρας ἐπαφεῖναι are paired alternatives; 'such as' with 'or' conveys this correctly.

last_rejected.quote: because their opposites are not numbered among our greatest goods
last_rejected.source_quote: διὰ τὸ μηδὲ τὰ ἀντικείμενα τούτοις, ἐν τοῖς μεγίστοις ἡμᾶς τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀριθμεῖν
last_rejected.why: The Greek says 'because we do not number even their opposites among our greatest goods'—the negation applies to 'their opposites' not being greatest goods, not to 'we do not number'. The English reverses: it says the opposites are not numbered among greatest goods, but the Greek says we don't count the opposites as among the greatest goods (i.e., health/wealth aren't the greatest goods).
last_rejected.fix: because we do not count even their opposites among our greatest goods
last_rejected.ruling: μηδὲ τὰ ἀντικείμενα...ἀριθμεῖν = 'not number their opposites among greatest goods'; English 'are not numbered' preserves meaning.
